planting.note: Plant dormant rhizomes an inch or two deep in spring once soil has warmed, in humus-rich, well-drained soil in filtered shade to part sun.

directions: This compact hidden-cone ginger carries broad, ruffled leaves marked with bold parallel red-and-cream stripes running out from the midrib, a pattern unusual among the generally plain-leaved Curcuma. Unlike many hidden gingers whose cone-shaped flower spike hides low among the foliage, this species pushes its red-and-white striped bracts up on a short stalk where the maroon-centered white true flowers are easy to see through late spring and summer. It prefers more shade than most Curcuma relatives and resents being baked in full afternoon sun, so site it under high tree canopy or on a shaded porch bed. Rhizomes go dormant and die back to the ground with cold; mulch heavily over winter in the cooler end of its range or lift and store rhizomes indoors where winters run colder than zone 8.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly in spring after soil has warmed, in rich, well-drained soil in bright shade; keep nearly dry during winter dormancy.

directions: This hybrid peacock ginger is grown chiefly for its oversized rosette of broad, platinum-and-blue-green marbled leaves with a rich maroon reverse, considerably larger than most other Kaempferia in cultivation. Clusters of orchid-like rosy pink flowers appear low at the soil line in spring before the foliage rosette has fully unfurled, then fade as the leaves take over for the display through summer and fall. It wants more shade than many gingers tolerate and performs best tucked beneath high canopy or on a shaded patio bed with steady moisture during active growth. Rhizomes go completely dormant and should be kept nearly dry over winter; mulch heavily or lift and store indoors outside its reliably hardy range.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in a sheltered spot with partial shade; mulch heavily over winter at the cold edge of its range.

directions: A smaller-growing ginger lily than many of its relatives, this variety stays under waist height and carries slender, spidery white flowers that age to pale primrose yellow, set off by prominent red stamens and red-tinted bracts. Flowers open from late summer into fall and carry a noticeable fragrance both by day and into the evening, making it a good choice near a shaded patio or walkway. It wants a sheltered site with dappled shade and protection from drying wind, and resents being baked in full Gulf Coast summer sun. Where winters dip into the colder end of zone 9, pile on a thick winter mulch to protect the dormant rhizomes, or lift and store them indoors.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
